newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG AND KNAUSS LEAD INTO 1997.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG AND KNAUSS LEAD INTO 1997.

text.p: Austrian Hans Knauss and Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg go into 1997 at the helm of the men's and women's Alpine skiing overall World Cup standings after a weekend of mixed fortunes for the duo.
Knauss, who has a good chance of becoming the first member of Austria's men's team to win the overall title since Karl Schranz in 1970, failed to finish Sunday's downhill in Bormio.
The 25-year-old from Schladming almost fell at the Carcentina curve halfway down the icy Stelvio piste when his skis slid from under him. He then retired.
The result left the all-rounder on 421 points, ahead of Frenchman Luc Alphand, who won the race but does not compete in the technical slalom disciplines, on 352.
The pressure on Knauss was eased by the absence of Norwegian rival Kjetil-Andre Aamodt, who decided to skip the race to recover strength for the major battles ahead.

Wiberg, seeking to become the first Swedish woman to capture the overall World Cup title, took the lead in the standings from Germany's Katja Seizinger at a slalom in the Austrian resort of Semmering, southwest of Vienna.

The 26-year-old Swede from Norrkoping, who now lives in Monte Carlo, was the winner on Saturday in Seizinger's absence and then increased her lead with a fourth place in Sunday's slalom behind Italian winner Deborah Compagnoni.
Otherwise the weekend rewarded familiar faces, with Italian and French racers having most to celebrate.

Alphand, already the most successful World Cup downhiller in French skiing history with eight wins, took his second victory of the season on the treacherous piste where he won early last year during the World Cup finals of the 1995 season.
Switzerland's William Besse was smiling after his second place gave his once-dominant country their first downhill podium finish for either of the sexes this season.
Italians had hoped to see one of their racers triumph in Bormio for the first time since the first World Cup race here in 1993 but they had to settle for Kristian Ghedina's third.
His compatriots were by then already celebrating Compagnoni's win in Austria -- the first slalom victory of her career -- which overshadowed all else.
The Olympic and world giant slalom champion kept her composure and performed two near-perfect runs on an icy Hrischenkogel piste in temperatures of minus 17 degrees celsius.
It was the eighth victory of her career -- which also includes the super-G gold at the 1992 Olympics.
Compagnoni missed the first half of last season when she was forced to undergo her third knee operation and she said she was pleased to have come through the summer unscathed.
France's Patricia Chauvet came second on Sunday with Austrian-born Claudia Riegler, who represents New Zealand after a dispute with the Austrian ski federation, third.
The women's circuit moves on to Maribor, Slovenia, for a giant slalom and slalom on Jan 3 and 4.
The men also resume in Slovenia with a giant slalom and slalom in Kranjska Gora on January 5 and 6.
